notes:
Docket sent you to the wrong page to fix your schema, and illustrated the problem with a field you already had.

When a site's LocalBusiness markup is missing properties, Docket lists them. That list has always been correct. Two things around it were not.

The first was the explanation. Whatever was missing, the sentence underneath said the same thing: hours drive the open/closed label, geo drives map placement, priceRange shows in the knowledge panel. On a hotel group we audited, the missing fields were telephone, opening hours, geo and image — and `priceRange`, the one example a reader could check in ten seconds, was the one property that site *does* publish. Meanwhile telephone and image, both genuinely absent, went unexplained. If you had checked the example you were given, you would have found it already on your page and concluded the whole finding was wrong. It was not: three of the four fields really were missing.

Docket now explains only the fields that are actually absent, and says nothing where it has nothing measured to say.

The second was the address. Docket judges the first LocalBusiness block it finds anywhere on the site, but it always printed your homepage as the place to fix it. On that same hotel group the homepage carries no LocalBusiness block at all — its only markup is an `Organization` — and the block being judged was on a city page several clicks away. The instruction was to complete a block on a page that did not have one. Docket now names the page the markup is actually on, in both the link and the fix.

**Broken links: the address written twice.** A link whose `href` carries `https://` twice over resolves to a URL whose host is the literal word "https". It fails like any dead link, and Docket used to report it beside genuinely dead destinations and advise you to find where the page had moved. Nothing had moved. On the site where we found it, deleting the duplicated scheme gives a URL that answers immediately with the PDF it was always meant to reach — a statutory disclosure document, unreachable since the day the link was published, with four correctly-written links to sibling documents beside it.

Docket now reports a doubled scheme as what it is — a typo in the link, with the address it was meant to be printed underneath — and stops counting it among your broken outbound links, which on that site took the count from two to one. Links that genuinely are dead are still reported exactly as before. A host that merely begins with the letters "http" is left alone.
